  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
# Anh's Watch

Anh Nguyen was sixty-three when he started at the fire department, a career he had pursued with the deliberate intention of putting himself in service to others, of being the one who ran toward danger rather than fleeing it. Now, at seventy-seven, he had been retired for fourteen years, but his mind had not let him retire from 1975. That was the year Saigon fell, the year Anh was twenty-five and caught in the chaos of the final evacuation—not as a soldier, but as a young man who had simply been in the wrong place when the artillery began.

He had been walking to his uncle's house that morning, crossing a street in District 1 when the first explosion came. Not the sound of it first—the pressure. A concussive force that lifted him off the ground and threw him backward into a storefront window. The glass had shattered around him, and in the seconds after, he remembered the smell: smoke and something burnt that he later understood was human flesh. Bodies lay in the street. Some were still moving. He had run then, not toward them but away, ashamed of his own survival even as he was running to preserve it.

For decades, Anh had built a life that looked whole. He married Linh, a woman who had also fled Vietnam and understood without needing to be told that some things were not discussed. He raised two children. He became a firefighter—a choice that seemed, to him, like atonement. He would save people. He would run toward the danger. For thirty years, he did this work with a steadiness that earned him respect, but it had cost him something he did not yet have words for.

The memory of that morning in 1975 had never left him. It lived in his body as a kind of permanent vigilance. In his fire department years, this had almost served him—he was alert, thorough, never complacent about hazards. But after he retired and the structure of duty fell away, the vigilance had nowhere to go. It turned inward.

Now, at night, Anh could not sleep. The thought of lying down, of closing his eyes in darkness, filled him with a dread so complete that he had taken to sleeping in the living room chair, the television on low, the room illuminated by its pale glow. Linh had stopped asking him to come to bed. When he did attempt to lie down, the memory came with a force that felt like an invasion—not a recollection he could control, but an assault. The explosion, the pressure, the smell, the bodies. The memory was so vivid, so detailed in its sensory completeness, that it seemed to belong to someone else entirely, not to the old man he had become. It was as if another person's trauma had been grafted into his mind.

Certain sounds could trigger it in the daytime too. An ambulance siren passing their house would send his heart into a panicked rhythm. He would find himself scanning the windows, checking the locks, looking for threats that his rational mind knew were not there. When Linh's nephew visited last month—his name was Duc, which was also the name of the uncle whose house Anh had been walking toward that day—Anh had felt a jolt of panic at simply hearing his name called from another room. He had excused himself and gone to the garage.

Over the months, a pattern had emerged. When Anh felt the memory beginning to surface, or when he heard a sound that threatened to trigger it, he would distract himself with fantasies of revenge. He imagined finding the soldiers responsible, imagined confrontations and violence that never came to satisfying conclusions. These fantasies had become a kind of compulsion, a way of converting his helplessness into a narrative where he had power. But they left him exhausted and ashamed.

What frightened Anh most was the thought that if he truly allowed himself to think about what happened, if he stopped running from it through distraction and avoidance and the small rituals of checking and scanning, he would not be able to handle it. He would break. He had survived by not breaking, and he had built a life on that survival, but the cost was that he had never actually stopped running. Now, at seventy-seven, with his wife growing frustrated at his withdrawal, with his children concerned about his isolation, Anh had come to his doctor and finally spoken the words: he could not go on like this. He did not know how to be a person anymore, only an object trying to survive. It was time, he thought, to stop running. But the thought of actually turning around and facing what was chasing him filled him with a terror he could barely name.
